stories.headline: Bihar MLC polls: Upper caste candidates dominate election results
stories.title: Bihar MLC polls: Upper caste candidates dominate election results
stories.summary: The Opposition Congress party which had put up its candidates on five seats has failed to win even a single seat in the elections
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'election results' in title weight 64
article_sentences: Out of eight State legislative Council seats which had gone to poll on October 23, 2026 and final results of them which were scheduled to be announced on October 27, some are new faces with upper caste dominating the poll on six seats while, the Backward caste and Extremely backward caste candidates won one seat each respectively from Kosi and Tirhut Graduate constituencies.

Out of eight seats, the upper-caste Bhumihar candidates won on five seats and one by a Rajput candidate while, the Other Backward (Yadav) and Extremely Backward Caste (mallah---boatmen/ Fishermen) candidates won on one seat each from Kosi and Tirhut Graduate constituencies.
The Opposition Congress party which had put up its candidates on five seats has failed to win even a single seat in the elections.

Five upper-caste Bhumihar candidates are Neeraj Kumar Singh (Patna Graduate), Sanjiv Kumar Singh (Patna Teachers), Suresh Rai (Darbhanga Teachers), Sarvesh Kumar (Darbhanga Graduate) and Narendra Singh (Tirhut Teachers).

Out of these five upper caste winning candidates, three Sarvesh Kumar (Darbhanga Graduate seat) and Narendra Singh (Tirhut Teachers seat), and from the other ruling coalition partner JD-U is Neeraj Kumar Singh from Patna Graduate seat are from ruling NDA bloc while, the other two from upper caste Bhumihar community are: Opposition Rashtriya Janata Dal Sanjiv Kumar from Patna Teachers seat and Jan Suraaj Party candidate Suresh Rai from Darbhanga Teachers seats.

One Independent candidate Rahul Raj from Saran Teachers constituency is from upper caste Rajput community while, Narendra Kumar Yadav from BJP from Kosi Graduate seat is from Other Backward Yadav (OBC) caste and the Extremely Backward Caste (EBC) candidate Vanshidhar Brajwasi is from mallah (boatman, Fishermen) community who won the poll from Tirhut Graduate seat as an Independent candidate.

Out of eight, the new faces are Sanjiv Kumar Singh from RJD, who won the Patna Teachers constituency, defeating the several-time MLC from the seat, Nawal Kishore Yadav from BJP, Suresh Rai from Jan Suraaj Party, who won from Darbhanga Teachers seat, defeating the veteran sitting Congress MLC Madan Mohan Jha, Rahul Raj, the Independent candidate from Saran Teachers constituency and the Tirhut Graduate constituency candidate Vanshidhar Brajwasi.

stories.headline: Ashok accuses State Election Commission of printing 90 lakh voter cards after announcement of SIR; SEC denies charge
stories.title: Ashok accuses State Election Commission of printing 90 lakh voter cards after announcement of SIR; SEC denies charge
stories.summary: Leader of Opposition in the Assembly R. Ashok has accused the State Election Commission of violating norms to facilitate irregularities in the proposed GBA polls by printing 90 lakh voters’ identity cards in Bengaluru at a cost of ₹20 crore after the announcement of Special Intensive Revision by the Election Commission of India
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Leader of Opposition in the Assembly R. Ashok has accused the State Election Commission (SEC) of violating norms to facilitate irregularities in the proposed GBA polls by printing 90 lakh voters’ identity cards in Bengaluru at a cost of ₹20 crore after the announcement of Special Intensive Revision (SIR) by the Election Commission of India.
Alleging that the Congress government was involved in these irregularities, Mr. Ashok demanded a CBI probe into the episode.
However, the SEC strongly denied these allegations by stating that the tenders had been floated before the announcement of SIR and that it had acted within its legal mandate.
Addressing a press conference in Bengaluru, Mr. Ashok alleged that the SEC had printed 90 lakh cards, though the total number of voters in Bengaluru had been pegged at around 59 lakh after the SIR.
Pointing out that the SEC was now left with an additional 31 lakh voters identity cards, he described these additional cards as “bogus” and alleged that they would be used for “vote theft”.
He alleged that the Congress government had got this done to commit irregularities in the proposed election to GBA.

“The State Election Commission did this though it had filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court stating that elections to local bodies would be held only after the SIR and after the new voters’ list is prepared,“ he said.
Denying the allegations, SEC Secretary Amaresh H. said the tender was called before the SIR was announced.
Mr. Amaresh said the tender was issued under Rule 26 of the Greater Bengaluru Governance (Registration of Electors) Rules, 2025, which provides for the printing of voter identity cards.
He said the SEC had acted within its legal mandate and that the SIR did not require it to suspend its work relating to local body electoral processes.
“The SIR is not binding on the State Election Commission in the manner being suggested.
Local body elections and elections conducted by the Election Commission of India are governed by different frameworks,” he said.

stories.headline: Cooperative Federalism: The Constitutional Compact India Must Renew
stories.title: Cooperative Federalism: The Constitutional Compact India Must Renew
stories.summary: India’s federalism is not a contest over who commands and who complies. It is a constitutional compact designed to reconcile national unity with regional autonomy, common purpose with political diversity, and effective governance with democratic accountability. Its success depends not on the concentration of power in one centre, but on the capacity of the Union and the States to exercise their respective constitutional responsibilities in partnership. As India confronts increasingly complex economic, environmental, technological and geopolitical challenges, cooperative federalism has become more than a constitutional aspiration. It is an essential condition of democratic stability, institutional trust and effective government. The constitutional scholar Granville Austin captured this distinctive design in The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation, describing India’s model as one of “cooperative federalism.” His insight remains relevant: India’s federal structure was shaped by the need to preserve national unity while accommodating an extraordinary diversity of languages, cultures, political traditions and regional aspirations. The constitutional challenge was never simply to distribute power, but to make that distribution work. The constitutional architecture of cooperation The Constitution does not expressly use the phrase “cooperative federalism,” but its institutional architecture reflects that philosophy. Article 1 describes India as a “Union of States.” Articles 245 and 246, read with the Seventh Schedule, distribute legislative powers between the Union and the States. Articles 256 and 257 address aspects of executive coordination, while Articles 268 to 293 govern financial relations. Article 263 provides for an Inter-State Council, and Article 280 establishes the Finance Commission. These provisions establish both the autonomy of constitutional authorities and the need for coordination. They do not envisage government as a collection of watertight compartments. The Constitution also gives the Union significant powers, reflecting the historical circumstances of Partition and the imperative of national integration. Yet this central strength must not be confused with an unrestricted authority to displace State autonomy. The constitutional framework requires a balance between national interests and the legitimate responsibilities of elected State governments. The Supreme Court’s decision in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) reinforced the constitutional significance of federalism, while the Court’s wider jurisprudence has emphasised that constitutional powers must be exercised within their prescribed limits. Federalism is therefore not merely an administrative arrangement. It is part of the constitutional structure through which democracy is organised, and power is held accountable. A strong Union requires strong States The false choice between a strong Union and strong States must be rejected. National unity is not weakened when States exercise legitimate autonomy; it is strengthened when regional aspirations find democratic expression within the constitutional framework. India’s federal experiment differs from federations formed through an agreement among previously sovereign political units. Its Constitution sought to preserve the unity of an exceptionally diverse country while assigning substantial responsibilities to different levels of government. That design requires flexibility, consultation and mutual respect. States are not administrative branches of the Union. They possess constitutionally defined powers and independent democratic mandates. Equally, State autonomy does not extinguish the Union’s responsibility for national security, macroeconomic stability and matters constitutionally entrusted to it. The objective must be constitutional partnership, not institutional rivalry. Political diversity must not become federal discrimination India’s democratic landscape is marked by different political parties governing at the Centre and across the States. This is neither an anomaly nor a constitutional inconvenience. It is a natural expression of electoral pluralism. The Constitution recognises governments formed through democratic processes, not governments entitled to cooperation only when their political affiliations coincide. A State government cannot be treated as an adversary merely because it belongs to the Opposition. Nor should legitimate access to national resources, institutional consultation or development opportunities depend on political alignment. The true test of cooperative federalism arises when governments disagree. Constitutional maturity lies in managing differences through dialogue, established institutions and law—not through confrontation, public recrimination or the politicisation of constitutional offices. Governments change; the federal compact must endure. Fiscal federalism: Autonomy requires resources The most consequential test of federalism is financial. States deliver many of the public services citizens experience directly, including healthcare, education, policing, agriculture, welfare and local infrastructure. Yet their ability to discharge these responsibilities depends substantially on the distribution of taxation powers, transfers and grants. A federation cannot function equitably if responsibilities are decentralised while financial discretion is disproportionately centralised. The Finance Commission is therefore a pivotal constitutional institution. Tax devolution and grants-in-aid must be guided by transparent principles that reconcile the needs of less-developed States, population-related responsibilities, fiscal discipline and developmental performance. States also require sufficient fiscal space to respond to local priorities and innovate in public policy. Predictable transfers, timely payments and meaningful consultation are essential to that autonomy. Fiscal federalism should not become a relationship between a permanent donor and a dependent recipient. It must recognise the States as partners in generating national prosperity and delivering constitutional promises. The GST Council: Cooperation without compulsory unanimity The Goods and Services Tax Council, established under Article 279A, offers an important institutional example. It brings the Union and the States into a common forum to deliberate on significant questions of indirect taxation and the functioning of the GST system. The experience has also exposed tensions over revenue compensation, fiscal autonomy, tax rates and the balance between uniformity and State flexibility. These disagreements do not necessarily indicate failure. Federal systems are designed to accommodate competing interests. The real test is whether institutional mechanisms permit disagreements to be negotiated fairly. The GST Council’s enduring lesson is that cooperation does not require unanimity on every question. It requires a genuine commitment to consultation, reasoned compromise and shared responsibility. Governors and the limits of constitutional discretion The office of the Governor presents another important test of federal balance. The Governor occupies a constitutional position within the parliamentary system, but the democratic legitimacy of State government ordinarily derives from its elected legislature and its majority in the Assembly. Questions concerning assent to Bills, government formation and the exercise of discretionary powers must be resolved through constitutional principles rather than partisan calculations. In State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab (2023), the Supreme Court underscored the importance of constitutional responsibility and the limits on gubernatorial inaction. The broader principle is that constitutional authorities must not frustrate the functioning of elected institutions through indefinite delay or an expansive interpretation of their discretion. The Governor is not an alternative political executive. The office must be exercised with restraint, neutrality and fidelity to the Constitution. Cooperative federalism requires every constitutional authority to respect the sphere of responsibility assigned to others. Cooperation for challenges that cross borders Competitive federalism has encouraged States to attract investment, improve infrastructure, generate employment and experiment with development strategies. Such competition can stimulate innovation and improve governance. But competition cannot substitute for cooperation where challenges transcend territorial boundaries. Air pollution moves across State borders. Rivers connect multiple jurisdictions. Migration, epidemics, energy security and transport infrastructure demand coordinated responses. Climate change, artificial intelligence and disaster management require shared standards, information and institutional capacity. India must therefore embrace competitive and cooperative federalism together: competition where it encourages better governance, and cooperation where common interests demand collective action. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated how closely national coordination and State-level implementation are connected. It also exposed the costs of inadequate consultation and uneven institutional capacity. The lesson extends to future public health emergencies, environmental crises and technological disruptions. Renewing the institutions of federal dialogue India already possesses institutions capable of strengthening this partnership, but their effectiveness depends on regular engagement and political will. The Inter-State Council under Article 263 should be used more consistently for structured discussion of Centre-State relations and inter-State disputes. The Finance Commission must retain its credibility as an impartial constitutional institution. The GST Council should remain a forum for meaningful negotiation, and NITI Aayog should facilitate substantive policy cooperation rather than merely communicate decisions already taken. Parliament, too, must give serious consideration to State perspectives when legislative proposals substantially affect their constitutional responsibilities. Consultation must occur early enough to influence policy. It cannot be reduced to a procedural formality after decisions have effectively been made. Constitutional morality and the road ahead Ultimately, cooperative federalism depends as much on constitutional morality as on institutional design. The Union must respect legitimate State autonomy; States must recognise legitimate national interests; Governors must act impartially; and elected governments must exercise their powers responsibly. Political parties must distinguish the interests of the Republic from the immediate advantages of partisan competition. The gravest threat to federalism is not disagreement. It is the erosion of institutional trust through the politicisation of constitutional powers. India’s federal compact must now be renewed through transparent fiscal arrangements, predictable intergovernmental cooperation, stronger consultation and scrupulous respect for constitutional boundaries. The question is not whether the Union or the States should prevail. It is whether both can discharge their responsibilities more effectively by working together. A confident India must be a confident Union of confident States. As Granville Austin’s understanding of cooperative federalism reminds us, national unity and regional autonomy need not be competing objectives. Properly balanced, they reinforce each other. Cooperative federalism is not a concession from the Union to the States. It is a constitutional obligation arising from the structure of the Republic. Renewing that compact is essential to India’s democratic credibility, developmental ambitions and constitutional future. (The Author is a Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of India, a public intellectual and a constitutional expert)

stories.headline: Adani eyes €3 billion acquisition of Dutch energy storage firm VTTI as supply disruptions boost demand
stories.title: Adani eyes €3 billion acquisition of Dutch energy storage firm VTTI as supply disruptions boost demand
stories.summary: Billionaire Gautam Adani, India’s richest person, is exploring a potential acquisition of Dutch energy storage group VTTI as supply disruptions make the facilities more valuable for energy trading, people familiar with the matter said.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Billionaire Gautam Adani, India’s richest person, is exploring a potential acquisition of Dutch energy storage group VTTI as supply disruptions make the facilities more valuable for energy trading, people familiar with the matter said.
Adani Group, the tycoon’s power-to-ports conglomerate, is among suitors that have been evaluating Rotterdam-based VTTI, according to the people.
A deal could value the company at around €3 billion ($3.4 billion), they said.
Australian infrastructure manager IFM Investors Pty and energy and commodities group Vitol SA each own around 45% of VTTI, while Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.
holds the remaining 10%.

Adnoc is considering selling out of VTTI completely and the other co-owners may also look to reduce their positions in the company in any deal, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing confidential information.
Deliberations are ongoing and there’s no certainty they’ll result in a transaction, the people said.
Other bidders have also been pursuing a stake in VTTI, they said.
A representative for Adani Group didn’t immediately respond to queries.
Spokespeople for IFM, Adnoc and VTTI declined to comment.
A representative for Vitol didn’t immediately comment.
VTTI operates terminals used to store fuels and chemicals, including fossil fuels, biofuels and solvents.

Adnoc is considering selling out of VTTI completely and the other co-owners may also look to reduce their positions in the company in any deal, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing confidential information.
Deliberations are ongoing and there’s no certainty they’ll result in a transaction, the people said.
Other bidders have also been pursuing a stake in VTTI, they said.
A representative for Adani Group didn’t immediately respond to queries.
Spokespeople for IFM, Adnoc and VTTI declined to comment.
